option1: It iterates List<ISubscriber> and calls notifyUser() polymorphically — each concrete subscriber's own override decides how it handles the notification
option2: It calls a static NotificationService.dispatch() method that internally branches on subscriber type
option3: It iterates List<User> and casts each element to check if it's Email or SMS before calling the right method
option4: It iterates a Map<String, ISubscriber> keyed by channel name
correctOptionExplanation: Polymorphism through the ISubscriber interface means the loop stays identical no matter how many or which subscriber types exist — each override supplies its own behavior.

option1: A StackOverflowError because super.notifyUser() re-invokes EmailSubscriber.notifyUser()
option2: "Email sending started to ___", then "notification upload completed on X", then "Email sending completed"
option3: Only the two Email lines — the super call is skipped since it's overridden
option4: "notification upload completed on X" printed first, then the two Email lines
correctOptionExplanation: super.notifyUser(message) explicitly calls the parent User implementation, executing in between the two println statements — not before or instead of them.

questionText: In Main.java, three subscribers (two EmailSubscriber, one SMSSubscriber) are added via channel.subscribe(...), then channel.uploadVideo(...) is called once. You now want a brand-new PushSubscriber to also get notified on the same event. What is the minimum change required inside YouTubeChannel.java itself?
option1: Add a new field List<PushSubscriber> pushSubscribers and loop over it separately
option2: Change subscribers from List<ISubscriber> to List<Object> so it can hold any subscriber type
option3: Zero changes — just create PushSubscriber implements ISubscriber and call channel.subscribe(new PushSubscriber(...))
option4: Add a new notifyPushSubscribers() private method and call it inside uploadVideo()
correctOptionExplanation: This is the core payoff of Observer: YouTubeChannel depends only on the ISubscriber abstraction, so new subscriber types plug in with zero modification to the subject.

questionText: EmailSubscriber(String email) never explicitly calls super(...), and User has no explicit constructor of its own either. Why does this still compile?
option1: email is treated as satisfying User's name field automatically via reflection
option2: ISubscriber provides a default constructor that EmailSubscriber inherits directly
option3: It doesn't compile — this is a bug in the course code
option4: Java inserts an implicit no-arg super() call to User's implicit default constructor
correctOptionExplanation: Every constructor's first line is implicitly super() unless another constructor call is written explicitly, and Java auto-generates a no-arg constructor for any class (like User) that declares none.

questionText: EmailSubscriber's constructor sets this.email = email but never touches User's name field or calls setName(...). Right after construction, what does mainak.getName() (cast to User) return?
option1: null — name was never assigned for this instance
option2: A NullPointerException at the getName() call
option3: "mg@gmail.com" — the constructor argument auto-assigns to the nearest matching field
option4: "Study with Mainak" — inherited from the channel
correctOptionExplanation: Fields aren't auto-populated from unrelated constructor parameters. name stays at its default value, null, since nothing ever assigns it.

questionText: You need to remove rajesh from the channel's subscriber list before a second video upload. You call channel.unsubscribe(rajesh). What does ISubject.unsubscribe(ISubscriber subscriber) rely on internally to find and remove the correct object?
option1: channel.subscribers.remove("rajesh") — matching by variable name string
option2: List.remove(Object), which uses equals()/reference identity to locate rajesh in the list
option3: Unsubscribing isn't possible once uploadVideo() has been called even once
option4: rajesh's index in the list, since ISubject only supports unsubscribe(int index)
correctOptionExplanation: YouTubeChannel.unsubscribe() calls subscribers.remove(subscriber), and ArrayList.remove(Object) walks the list comparing with equals() (defaulting to reference equality here since ISubscriber implementers don't override equals()).

questionText: EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber both override notifyUser() with a near-identical shape: print a start message, call super.notifyUser(), print a completion message — only the wording and fields differ. What existing course pattern would remove this duplication without changing the ISubscriber interface?
option1: It's fine as-is; repeating a similar shape across two classes isn't worth fixing
option2: Make notifyUser() static in User so both subclasses share one implementation automatically
option3: Pull the start/complete wrapper into a final template method in User, leaving only the middle piece (channel-specific start/complete text) as abstract hooks — the same idea as class-16/17's Template Method
option4: Merge EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber into a single class with an if(type.equals("email")) branch
correctOptionExplanation: This is a genuine Template Method opportunity layered on top of Observer: fix the skeleton (start → core notify → complete) in the base class, vary only the hook text per subclass.

questionText: If YouTubeChannel.subscribers were changed from List<ISubscriber> to List<User>, what concretely degrades, given EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber both extend User?
option1: notifyUser() would silently stop being called since User doesn't override it
option2: It would force every subscriber to be re-cast to ISubscriber inside notifyUser()
option3: It's a compile error immediately, since EmailSubscriber no longer satisfies List<User>
option4: The channel now depends on the concrete User class instead of the ISubscriber abstraction — a brand-new subscriber type implementing ISubscriber directly (without extending User) could no longer be subscribed
correctOptionExplanation: Coupling the subject to a concrete class instead of the interface reintroduces exactly the rigidity Observer is meant to remove — this violates DIP even though it still compiles and runs.

questionText: notifySubscribers() is private inside YouTubeChannel. A subclass PremiumYouTubeChannel extends YouTubeChannel wants to add logging every time subscribers are notified. Can it override notifySubscribers() to do this?
option1: No — private methods aren't inherited or overridable; the subclass would need notifySubscribers to be protected first, or it must override uploadVideo() entirely instead
option2: No, because notifySubscribers is also implicitly final
option3: Yes, because private only restricts external callers, not subclasses
option4: Yes, any method can be overridden as long as the subclass is in the same package
correctOptionExplanation: Private methods are invisible to subclasses entirely — not just "not overridable." PremiumYouTubeChannel would need to override the public uploadVideo() and reimplement the loop, or the base class would need to expose a protected hook.

questionText: A teammate proposes skipping ISubject/ISubscriber and hardcoding two fields in YouTubeChannel: List<EmailSubscriber> emailSubs and List<SMSSubscriber> smsSubs, with uploadVideo() looping over both. What's the concrete cost versus the real interface-based code?
option1: It would break EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber's constructors
option2: Adding a third subscriber type (like PushSubscriber) now requires a new field, a new loop inside uploadVideo(), and editing YouTubeChannel.java itself — the real ISubscriber-based code needs zero changes there
option3: It would make unsubscribe() faster since each list is smaller
option4: No real cost — it performs identically since both approaches loop over lists
correctOptionExplanation: This is the classic "closed for extension" failure: every new subscriber type means touching the subject's source code again, which is exactly what the interface-based design avoids.

questionText: Imagine a WeatherStation (Subject) that notifies a CurrentConditionsDisplay and a StatisticsDisplay (Observers) whenever temperature changes, mirroring YouTubeChannel's structure. Why should WeatherStation's notify loop hold a List<IDisplay> rather than separate fields for each concrete display?
option1: Because separate fields would require making WeatherStation abstract
option2: There's no real benefit — separate fields would work identically for any number of displays
option3: So new display types (e.g. a ForecastDisplay) can subscribe without WeatherStation's source code changing at all — same reasoning as the real ISubscriber list
option4: Because Java doesn't allow more than one field of the same generic type in a class
correctOptionExplanation: Same rationale as class-21: a single collection typed to the interface keeps the subject open to new observer types without modification.

questionText: A stock ticker Subject notifies a MobileApp, a WebDashboard, and an EmailAlert observer on every price change, structured just like YouTubeChannel/ISubscriber. If EmailAlert's onPriceChange() throws an unchecked exception midway through the notify loop (structured like YouTubeChannel's for-each), what happens to MobileApp and WebDashboard if they're later in the list?
option1: They still get notified normally, since each observer's notify call runs on its own separate thread by default
option2: The Subject automatically catches the exception and continues to the next observer
option3: Only the throwing observer is skipped; the loop resumes at the next index automatically
option4: They never get notified for that event — an uncaught exception propagates out of the for-each loop and stops it before reaching the remaining observers
correctOptionExplanation: A plain for-each loop like notifySubscribers() has no built-in exception isolation — one misbehaving observer can silently break notification for everyone after it in the list. This is a real design risk worth guarding against (e.g. try/catch inside the loop).

questionText: In an order-tracking system, an Order (Subject) notifies a Customer, a WarehouseSystem, and a LogisticsSystem (Observers) whenever its status changes, following the same subscribe/notify shape as YouTubeChannel. A new requirement appears: only WarehouseSystem should be notified when status becomes "CANCELLED", not the other two. What does this reveal about a plain Observer implementation like the course's?
option1: The plain Observer notifies everyone on every event uniformly — filtering which observers care about which event types isn't handled by ISubject/ISubscriber alone and needs extra logic (e.g. passing an event type observers can check)
option2: This can only be solved by switching to the Strategy pattern instead of Observer
option3: This proves Observer is the wrong pattern entirely for order tracking
option4: Nothing — ISubject already supports per-observer event filtering out of the box
correctOptionExplanation: Observer's base contract is "notify all registered observers," not "notify only interested observers." Selective/filtered notification is a real extension point, not something notifyUser(String) gives you automatically.

questionText: A single ISubscriber instance is registered to two different YouTubeChannel objects (e.g. subscribed to both "Study with Mainak" and a second channel). Inside notifyUser(String message), how does that subscriber know which channel the notification came from, given the real method signature is notifyUser(String message)?
option1: Each YouTubeChannel spawns a separate thread per subscriber, so the subscriber can check Thread.currentThread().getName()
option2: It can't, as written — the message string is the only information passed; distinguishing the source channel would require changing the signature (e.g. notifyUser(String channelName, String message)) or passing the Subject itself
option3: notifyUser() is called twice — once per channel — with the channel object substituted into the message
option4: ISubscriber automatically receives a reference to the calling YouTubeChannel via a hidden parameter
correctOptionExplanation: This is a legitimate limitation of the current minimal signature. It's exactly the kind of design gap worth pointing out: Observer doesn't guarantee source identification unless the contract is built to carry it.

questionText: A test wants to verify that YouTubeChannel.uploadVideo() actually calls notifyUser() on every subscribed observer, without depending on real email/SMS sending. What's the cleanest way to do this, using the existing ISubscriber interface?
option1: Directly access YouTubeChannel's private subscribers list via reflection and manually invoke notifyUser() on each
option2: Modify YouTubeChannel to add a public getLastNotifiedMessage() method just for the test
option3: Create a lightweight test class implementing ISubscriber that just records whether notifyUser() was called (and with what message), subscribe it, then assert on it — no changes needed to YouTubeChannel
option4: It's not testable without also spinning up real Email and SMS services
correctOptionExplanation: This is the practical payoff of coding to ISubscriber: a test double is just another class implementing the same tiny interface — no test-specific changes to the subject are needed at all.

option1: An empty string ""
option2: It throws a NullPointerException on construction
option4: null
correctOptionExplanation: Same reasoning as the EmailSubscriber name question: nothing in the constructor path ever assigns User.name, so it holds its default value of null. No exception is thrown just from having a null field.

questionText: channel.subscribe(mainak) is called where mainak is declared as ISubscriber mainak = new EmailSubscriber(...). Why is the variable declared as ISubscriber mainak rather than EmailSubscriber mainak, given both compile fine for the subscribe() call?
option1: Declaring against the interface keeps the client code (Main) decoupled from the concrete subscriber type, matching how YouTubeChannel itself only depends on ISubscriber — useful if mainak's type needs to change later or is chosen dynamically
option2: EmailSubscriber mainak would actually fail to compile since subscribe() only accepts ISubscriber
option3: It's required because ISubscriber is declared as a sealed interface
option4: There is no real difference — it's purely a stylistic preference with zero design implication
correctOptionExplanation: channel.subscribe(ISubscriber subscriber) would happily accept an EmailSubscriber-typed variable too (via polymorphism); declaring the variable itself as ISubscriber is a program-to-the-interface habit, not a compiler requirement here.

questionText: A GUI button in a desktop app lets multiple listeners register via button.addClickListener(listener), and clicking the button notifies every registered listener — structurally identical to channel.subscribe()/uploadVideo(). What role does the Button play in Observer-pattern terms, and what role does each listener play?
option1: Button and each listener are both Subjects communicating peer-to-peer
option2: Button is the Subject (like YouTubeChannel); each listener is an Observer/Subscriber (like ISubscriber implementers)
option3: Button is the Observer; each listener is a Subject
option4: This isn't Observer at all — it's a form of the Adapter pattern since click events get "adapted" into listener calls
correctOptionExplanation: Any "register interested parties, then broadcast an event to all of them" shape is Observer, regardless of domain — GUI listener registration is one of the most common real-world instances of it.

questionText: In the real code, YouTubeChannel.uploadVideo() does its own upload logic first ("uploading video to X"), then explicitly calls notifySubscribers(...) as its last line, with a comment "//must notify" above it. What would happen, functionally, if that notifySubscribers(...) call were accidentally deleted?
option1: subscribers list would automatically empty itself since it's never read
option2: EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber would throw exceptions on the next uploadVideo() call
option3: The video "uploads" (its own println runs) but no subscriber ever hears about it — subscribe()/unsubscribe() still work, but the notify half of the contract silently stops firing
option4: The program would fail to compile, since ISubject requires notifySubscribers() to be called inside every public method
correctOptionExplanation: Nothing enforces that a Subject actually calls notify — ISubject only requires subscribe/unsubscribe to exist. Forgetting the notify call is a pure logic bug, not something the type system catches, which is worth flagging as a real footgun.

questionText: Compare the real EmailSubscriber/SMSSubscriber (which extend User and override notifyUser(), calling super.notifyUser() in the middle) to a hypothetical version where EmailSubscriber instead HELD a User field (composition) and delegated to it manually. What's the main tradeoff of the inheritance version actually used in the course code?
option1: The inheritance version is strictly worse in every case and should never be used here
option2: There is no tradeoff — inheritance and composition behave identically in this exact case
option3: The composition version wouldn't compile since ISubscriber requires extending a concrete class
option4: Inheritance gives free reuse of User's notifyUser() body via super, but tightly couples EmailSubscriber to User's implementation — composition would let EmailSubscriber swap or avoid that implementation entirely, at the cost of writing the delegation manually
correctOptionExplanation: This mirrors the classic composition-over-inheritance discussion from earlier in the course (e.g. duck examples) — the real code chose inheritance for convenience/reuse, which is a legitimate but not free choice.

questionText: If ISubject's method were changed from subscribe(ISubscriber subscriber) to subscribe(String subscriberType, String contactInfo) — having YouTubeChannel internally construct the right EmailSubscriber or SMSSubscriber based on the string — what design problem would this reintroduce?
option1: YouTubeChannel would need an if-else (or switch) branching on subscriberType to decide which concrete class to instantiate — the exact type-checking YouTubeChannel currently avoids entirely by accepting a ready-made ISubscriber
option2: This would make YouTubeChannel violate the Single Responsibility Principle only, with no coupling issue
option3: Nothing changes — this would be functionally and structurally identical to the current design
option4: It would only be a problem if there were more than 10 subscriber types
correctOptionExplanation: This reframes the "bad code" alternative you already discussed conceptually: pushing object-creation responsibility (and the type-branching that comes with it) into the Subject recreates the if-else explosion Observer avoids.

questionText: A chat room Subject broadcasts every incoming message to all connected ChatParticipant observers, structured just like uploadVideo() → notifySubscribers(). If a participant disconnects but the app forgets to call unsubscribe() on their ChatParticipant object, what concrete problem results, tracing through the real subscribe/unsubscribe mechanics?
option1: The next uploadVideo()-style broadcast call throws a NullPointerException and halts
option2: The stale ChatParticipant reference stays in the subscribers list and keeps getting notifyUser() calls forever (a dangling-reference / memory-leak-style bug), since nothing but an explicit unsubscribe() call removes it
option3: The JVM automatically detects the disconnected socket and removes the observer from the list
option4: ISubject silently ignores disconnected observers based on a built-in heartbeat check
correctOptionExplanation: Observer's list only shrinks via explicit unsubscribe() calls — there's no automatic cleanup. Forgetting to unsubscribe on disconnect/teardown is a very real, very common bug class in Observer-based systems.

option1: This is a mistake in the course code — ISubject should declare notify() as well
option2: ISubject implicitly requires every implementer to call notify() inside every public method, enforced at compile time
option3: ISubject only guarantees that implementers can register/deregister observers — it says nothing about when or how notification happens; that's entirely up to each Subject's own event methods (like uploadVideo())
option4: Without a notify() method in the interface, subscribers can never actually be notified
correctOptionExplanation: The interface only standardizes the subscription mechanics; the decision of which domain events (uploadVideo, cancelOrder, priceChange, etc.) trigger notification is left to each concrete Subject — that's intentional, not an oversight.

questionText: A news agency AP-style Subject broadcasts breaking-news events to registered NewsOutlet observers (TV station, radio station, website). If NewsOutlet were an abstract class instead of an interface, with a concrete default notifyUser() that just prints the message, what would TVStation still be forced to do to add its own "breaking news banner" behavior on top?
option1: Nothing extra; abstract classes automatically merge subclass and parent behavior without an override
option2: Abstract classes cannot have concrete methods, so this scenario is impossible in Java
option3: Declare a second method notifyUserTV() since notifyUser() can't be overridden once it has a body
option4: Override notifyUser(), and — if it wants the default printing behavior too — explicitly call super.notifyUser() from inside its override, exactly like EmailSubscriber does with User
correctOptionExplanation: An abstract class can mix abstract and concrete methods freely; a concrete method with a body still follows normal override + optional super-call rules, same as User.notifyUser() here.

questionText: Suppose two teams independently subscribe the exact same EmailSubscriber object instance to a YouTubeChannel by calling channel.subscribe(sameInstance) twice (no check for duplicates in the real subscribe() code). What happens on the next uploadVideo() call?
option1: That subscriber's notifyUser() gets called twice for the same event, since the ArrayList now holds the same reference in two separate slots and the for-each loop visits both
option2: The second subscribe() call is a silent no-op, since List prevents duplicate references by default
option3: Only the last subscribe() call's registration counts; the first is overwritten in place
option4: The second subscribe() call throws an IllegalStateException
correctOptionExplanation: YouTubeChannel.subscribe() just calls subscribers.add(subscriber) with no duplicate check — ArrayList happily stores the same reference multiple times, so notifyUser() really does fire twice. Worth flagging as a real gap in the minimal implementation.

questionText: In User.java, notifyUser(String message) is a public instance method with a body (not abstract), yet EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber both still choose to override it rather than reuse it directly. If a third subscriber type, WhatsAppSubscriber extends User, is created but does NOT override notifyUser() at all, what happens when it's notified?
option1: It fails to compile, since ISubscriber requires every implementer to explicitly override notifyUser()
option2: It uses User's own notifyUser() implementation as-is, printing "notification " + message — perfectly valid, since overriding is optional, not required
option3: It throws an AbstractMethodError at runtime since User.notifyUser() is meant to be a placeholder
option4: It silently does nothing, since only overridden methods actually execute
correctOptionExplanation: Overriding is opt-in. A subclass that doesn't override an inherited concrete method just uses the parent's implementation unchanged — there's nothing broken about that.

questionText: A ride-hailing Driver (Subject) notifies subscribed RiderApp instances whenever the driver's location updates, using the same subscribe/notify shape as YouTubeChannel. If this happens 10 times per second per driver, what specific cost does the current synchronous for-each notify loop (like notifySubscribers()) impose that YouTubeChannel's once-per-upload use case doesn't really surface?
option1: There's no additional cost — loop iteration cost is O(1) regardless of call frequency
option2: ISubscriber would need to be converted into an abstract class to handle high-frequency updates
option3: Each notify() call blocks until every subscriber's notifyUser() returns, so a slow subscriber (e.g. one doing network I/O) delays notification of everyone after it in the list, and this cost compounds at high frequency
option4: The list would need to become a Set to avoid duplicate notifications automatically
correctOptionExplanation: The synchronous, sequential nature of the real for-each loop is fine for occasional events like a video upload, but at high frequency the cost of slow subscribers blocking the whole notify cycle becomes a real, visible bottleneck — a legitimate scaling consideration, distinct from any multithreading implementation detail.

option1: Field initialization would fail to compile because ArrayList requires a constructor argument
option2: Constructor initialization is required specifically because ISubject declares subscribers as abstract
option3: It matters a lot — initializing in the constructor makes subscribers shared across all YouTubeChannel instances, unlike field initialization
option4: Functionally it doesn't matter here — both approaches produce a freshly initialized empty list before the constructor body finishes running for each YouTubeChannel object; it's a stylistic choice, not a correctness issue
correctOptionExplanation: Both field initializers and constructor-body assignment run once per object before the constructor finishes (field initializers actually run first) — there's no sharing-across-instances risk either way since this isn't static.

questionText: A logging framework has Logger (Subject) notifying registered LogAppender observers (ConsoleAppender, FileAppender, DatabaseAppender) on every log event — the same subscribe/notify shape as class-21. If DatabaseAppender's notifyUser()-equivalent method needs to know the log's severity level (INFO/ERROR/etc.), but the shared interface method signature is only append(String message), what's the real constraint being hit, and how would you actually fix it?
option1: The interface method signature limits what data observers receive — fix it by widening the shared method's signature (e.g. append(String level, String message) or passing a small LogEvent object) so every observer, not just DatabaseAppender, gets the extra context
option2: DatabaseAppender should just embed the severity level inside the message string using string parsing on the receiving end
option3: There's no fix possible — DatabaseAppender would need to abandon the Observer pattern entirely and poll Logger directly instead
option4: This is solved automatically by making Logger extend Thread so severity is passed via thread-local storage
correctOptionExplanation: This is the same signature-carries-everything constraint as the earlier "which channel did this come from" question — Observer notifications can only carry what the shared method signature carries, so real fixes touch the interface, not the individual observer.

questionText: In the real class-21 code, User implements ISubscriber and both EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber extend User. If ISubscriber instead had TWO methods — notifyUser(String message) and getContactInfo() — what would concretely change about how much EmailSubscriber and SMSSubscriber are each forced to implement, compared to today's single-method interface?
option1: It would force ISubscriber to become an abstract class instead of an interface
option2: Each subclass (or User itself) would now need to implement getContactInfo() too, since implementing an interface means providing bodies for every one of its abstract methods, not just the ones a given class cares about
option3: Only EmailSubscriber would need getContactInfo(); SMSSubscriber would be exempt since phoneNumber already exists
option4: Nothing changes — Java interfaces only require overriding whichever methods a class chooses to use
correctOptionExplanation: Every abstract method in an interface is mandatory for any implementing class (directly or via an inherited implementation) — this is also a natural segue to why ISP matters: a bloated ISubscriber forces every implementer to carry methods it may not need.
